summary:
Syria is a country trans visitors should not enter. The 1949 Penal Code remains the operative legal framework after the fall of the Assad regime in December 2024. Article 520 criminalises "carnal relations against the order of nature" with up to three years' imprisonment, and Article 517 criminalises public indecency. Both provisions are applied to women as well as men, so the gender a visitor presents does not place them outside their scope.

An updated country overview published by Outright International on 12 March 2026 records the same legal position and adds two findings that matter at the border and after it: legal gender recognition is impossible, so a passport or identity document cannot be brought into line with a visitor's gender, and LGBTI organisations cannot register, so there is no domestic organisation able to offer a trans visitor assistance, shelter or legal representation.

No anti-discrimination protection exists in Syrian law. The state's response to same-sex conduct is criminalisation, not protection, and nothing in the current framework prohibits discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity in employment, services, housing or policing. A trans visitor who turns to the authorities for help is entering the same legal system that criminalises them.

Enforcement has historically been carried out by raid. In June 2010 Syrian authorities raided private parties over a period of weeks, arresting more than 25 men in a single swoop on charges including homosexual acts, encouraging homosexual behaviour and organising obscene parties. Several of those arrested also faced drug charges. The raids targeted private gatherings rather than public conduct, which is relevant to a visitor's assumption that staying indoors lowers exposure.

Violence by non-state armed actors compounds the statutory position. A 2018 Human Rights Watch report on LGBT activism across the Middle East and North Africa records that the Islamic State had claimed at least 16 killings in Syria for alleged sodomy as of June 2016, alongside 23 in Iraq and 3 in Libya. The same documentation records the Islamic State reporting the execution of at least 30 people for "sodomy" in the areas it controlled, an issue raised at the United Nations Security Council in August 2015 in the Council's first discussion of LGBT concerns. Beatings and torture of LGBT people are recorded as frequent, including attacks attributed to Hay'at Tahrir al-Sham as well as the Islamic State.

Political rhetoric across the opposition spectrum has endorsed harsher treatment rather than protection. A Free Syrian Army member stated publicly that he would enforce tougher laws and would not object to stoning homosexuals, while a secular opposition leader said Syrian society would answer "no way" to gay people claiming rights. These statements came from actors opposed to the Assad government, which indicates that a change of government did not by itself deliver a protective legal culture.

Health care access is filtered through official stigma. In 2005 the Deputy Minister of Religious Endowments publicly described HIV/AIDS as "divine punishment" for fornication and homosexuality. The Health Ministry claimed at the same time that only 369 people were infected and offered free medicines; NGOs estimated that figure to be at least five times too low, and the United Nations chastised the government for ineffective prevention. The state runs voluntary HIV testing clinics, distributes pamphlets, tolerates the work of some NGOs and offers a limited HIV/AIDS education program in secondary schooling, but comprehensive public education for LGBTQ people does not exist. Prevalence was recorded as under 2 per 100,000 in the general population and under 1% among most-at-risk populations in 2018, with 1,013 reported cases through the third quarter of 2019 since the first reported infections in 1987. Physical safety is itself a barrier to care, since seeking treatment risks exposure.

One incident from the post-Assad period requires care in how it is reported. In April 2025 the Syrian organisation Guardians of Equality Movement, working through a network of on-the-ground reporters, investigated a report claiming that LGBTQIA+ individuals were being hunted and targeted in Homs and found it inaccurate. The organisation published the finding to avoid stirring incitement against the community. The existence of the rumour is not evidence of a massacre; the criminal provisions and the armed-group violence documented above are the sourced basis for the risk assessment here.
tangentialFactors:
Public LGBTQ expression in Syria has been squeezed to the point of disappearance since the civil war. The region's only gay tour, which ran through Damascus and Aleppo, stopped operating; its organiser described the hammams used as venues before 2011 as "a paradise for gay people" where "we never had any problems." The underground LGBTQ hubs of Damascus have been eradicated. A visitor planning around any social scene should assume none exists in public form.

Digital expression persists under conditions of anonymity. The "One of you" movement began on Facebook in March 2020 and moved to Twitter, with university students painting LGBTQ flag colours on their fingers and photographing themselves under a faculty building. Most participants used fake accounts for fear of identification. Reactions ranged from defence to threats of blood before the movement faded amid COVID-19.

Comparative context from the same period: the Human Rights Watch tallies place Syria's 16 claimed killings for alleged sodomy behind Iraq's 23 and above Libya's 3 as of June 2016, with the Islamic State's own reported executions in Syria numbered at least 30.

Older state conduct is documented by contemporaneous reporting. PinkNews reported on 23 June 2010 that Syrian authorities had raided several private gay parties over the preceding weeks, arresting more than 25 men in the latest operation.

Earlier official hostility to LGBT people was expressed through public health messaging as well as policing, most starkly in the 2005 statement by the Deputy Minister of Religious Endowments that HIV/AIDS was divine punishment for homosexuality, made while the Health Ministry was simultaneously offering free antiretroviral medicines.
localsOnly:
Syrian LGBT people describe concealment as the ordinary condition of life. Amira al-Tabbaa, a 36-year-old interviewed by Syria Direct in October 2020, said that in Damascus she met friends in gay-friendly cafes and lived "only in whispers." The criminal provisions and the 2010 party raids set the background for that caution, and the closure of Damascus's underground hubs after 2011 removed what social infrastructure existed.

Residents have no access to legal gender recognition and cannot register LGBTI organisations, so there is no domestic mechanism for document correction, collective advocacy or formal complaint. Organisers work anonymously or from abroad.

Health provision exists in narrow form: voluntary HIV testing clinics, free medicines, pamphlet distribution, tolerated NGO work and a limited HIV/AIDS program in secondary schools. There is no comprehensive public education covering LGBTQ people. Activists have drawn attention to killings to the international level, including at a United Nations Security Council session on LGBT rights in 2015, at which gay refugees from Syria and Iraq described constant fear of violence and death under authoritarian governments, militant groups and the Islamic State.

Discrimination is also carried into exile: Syrian LGBTQ+ refugees in host countries report exclusion based on race, language, skin colour and religious background, in addition to their displacement status.
outOfScopeNotes:
The European Union Agency for Asylum's Syria country focus entry on the treatment of state, non-state and societal actors records no usable finding for this assessment. It was reviewed and contributed nothing that could be cited.

Two figures for Islamic State killings of people accused of sodomy in Syria appear in the inventory and are not reconciled by the sources: Human Rights Watch tallied at least 16 claimed killings as of June 2016, while separate documentation records the group reporting executions of at least 30 people in the areas it controlled. The discrepancy is unresolved and may reflect different counting periods or definitions.

The inventory does not establish how the interim authorities governing Syria since December 2024 are currently enforcing Articles 520 and 517 in practice, at what level, or against which categories of person. The legal provisions are current; enforcement frequency is not documented here.

The Guardians of Equality Movement's April 2025 report is the only post-transition source in the inventory. Its single recorded finding is a debunking of the Homs hunting claim. Whether it documents other incidents of violence against trans people specifically is unresolved and not sourced in this pass.

Whether a trans visitor can enter Syria on documents that conflict with their presentation is unresolved. The impossibility of legal gender recognition inside the country is sourced; the border and visa consequences are not.
